name: Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort, Headless, ExternalName
objective: CKAD › Services & Networking. Drill every Service shape and the Ingress/endpoints surface: ClusterIP with named targetPort, NodePort on a pinned port, headless, ExternalName, sessionAffinity, Ingress (pathType/ingressClassName/TLS), a selector-less Service + manual EndpointSlice, and a no-hint 'no endpoints' diagnose-fix. Graded exactly.

questions.title: ClusterIP with a named targetPort
questions.teach:
`targetPort` can be a **named** container port instead of a number — handy when the port number may change. Just set `targetPort: http` to match the container's named port.

**Gotcha:** the name must exactly match the container's port name, not the number.
questions.prompt:
A Deployment `web` (label `app=web`, container port **named `http`** = 80) runs in `svcnet-learn`. Create a **ClusterIP** Service `web-svc` with `port: 80` whose `targetPort` is the **named** port `http`, selecting `app=web`.

Target: `web-svc` ClusterIP, port 80 → targetPort `http`, selector app=web.
questions.hint: `targetPort: http` (the name, not 80). `kubectl -n svcnet-learn expose deployment web --name web-svc --port 80 --target-port http`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n svcnet-learn expose deployment web --name web-svc --port 80 --target-port http
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints web-svc

verification.description: web-svc ClusterIP port 80 -> targetPort 'http', selector app=web

questions.eli5:
A **Service** is like the front desk of an office building. Clients call the front desk's single, stable number (the Service) and the desk forwards them to whichever employee (pod) is free. The clients never need to know the employees' personal extensions, which change all the time.

A **ClusterIP** Service is the most basic kind: it has an internal phone number only people *inside* the building can dial. It has two port numbers:

- **port** — the number callers dial *at the desk* (here `80`).
- **targetPort** — the extension the desk *forwards to* on the pod.

The neat trick here: instead of forwarding to a numeric extension, you forward to a **named** one. The pod's container labelled its port `http`, so you set `targetPort: http`. The desk looks up whatever number `http` currently points to. If the team later moves `http` from 80 to 8080, your Service keeps working untouched.

`kubectl expose deployment web --name web-svc --port 80 --target-port http -n svcnet-learn` builds it, and its `selector: app=web` is how the desk knows which employees to forward to.

**Watch out for:**

- `targetPort: http` must match the container's **port name exactly** — it's the *name*, not the number. A typo or using `80` when the task says "named" is wrong.
- The Service finds pods by **selector**, and the pod must actually have a port **named** `http` for the name to resolve. No such name → no working target.
- Verify it wired up with `kubectl get endpoints web-svc`: if it's empty, the selector didn't match any pods.
- `port` (what clients dial) and `targetPort` (the container's port) are two different things — don't collapse them.
questions.deepDive:
## ClusterIP with a named targetPort — full rundown

### Mental model
A **Service** gives a stable virtual IP + DNS name in front of a changing set of pods selected by labels. **ClusterIP** (the default type) is reachable only inside the cluster. `port` is the Service's listening port; `targetPort` is the pod port traffic is forwarded to — and `targetPort` may be a **named** container port, decoupling the Service from the pod's numeric port.

### Named port on the pod
```yaml
# Deployment pod template
    ports:
    - name: http          # <- the name
      containerPort: 80
```
### The Service
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-svc, namespace: svcnet-learn }
spec:
  type: ClusterIP          # default; may be omitted
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
  - port: 80               # Service port (what clients hit)
    targetPort: http       # named container port (resolved per-pod)
```
Imperative:
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn expose deployment web \
  --name web-svc --port 80 --target-port http
```

### port vs targetPort vs nodePort
| Field | Lives on | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `port` | the Service (ClusterIP) | port clients connect to |
| `targetPort` | the pod | container port traffic is sent to (number **or** name) |
| `nodePort` | each node | only for `type: NodePort`/`LoadBalancer` |

> If `targetPort` is omitted it defaults to `port`.

### Why named targetPort
Each pod can map the same name to a different number. The Service resolves `http` **per pod** via its container port spec — so changing the number in the Deployment doesn't require touching the Service.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-svc
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints web-svc        # should list pod IPs:80
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web-svc
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-svc \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].targetPort}{"\n"}'   # http
```
Empty endpoints ⇒ selector matched no pods, or no pod exposes a port named `http`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- `targetPort: http` is the **name**, must exactly match the container's `ports[].name`. Using `80` fails a "named" requirement.
- The pod **must declare** a port with that name; otherwise the name can't resolve and endpoints stay empty.
- `port` ≠ `targetPort` — the Service port and container port are independent.
- `expose` copies the Deployment's selector automatically; hand-written YAML must set `selector` yourself.
- ClusterIP is cluster-internal only — not reachable from outside without NodePort/Ingress/port-forward.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn expose deployment web \
  --name web-svc --port 80 --target-port http
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints web-svc
```

questions.title: NodePort on a pinned port
questions.teach:
A **NodePort** Service (`type: NodePort`) opens a port on every node. Pin it with `nodePort: 30080` instead of letting one be auto-assigned.

**Gotcha:** `nodePort` must fall in the 30000–32767 range.
questions.prompt:
Create a **NodePort** Service `web-np` for `app=web`: `port: 80`, `targetPort: 80`, pinned `nodePort: 30080`.

Target: `web-np` type NodePort, port 80 → 80, nodePort 30080, selector app=web.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn create service nodeport web-np --tcp=80:80 --node-port=30080` then set its selector to app=web (or edit), OR write YAML with `type: NodePort` and `nodePort: 30080`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-np, namespace: svcnet-learn }
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80, nodePort: 30080 } ]
YAML

verification.description: web-np NodePort port 80 -> 80, nodePort 30080, selector app=web

questions.eli5:
A plain ClusterIP front desk only takes calls from *inside* the building. A **NodePort** Service adds a public doorbell: it opens the **same port number on every node (every door of the building)**, so someone outside can ring any door and get forwarded to a pod inside.

There are now three port numbers in play:

- **nodePort** — the public doorbell on each node (here pinned to `30080`).
- **port** — the internal Service port (`80`), still usable from inside.
- **targetPort** — the pod's container port the traffic finally reaches (`80`).

Normally Kubernetes picks a random doorbell number for you; here you **pin** it to `30080` so it's predictable.

`type: NodePort` plus `nodePort: 30080` and a `selector: app=web` does it.

**Watch out for:**

- The pinned `nodePort` **must be in the 30000–32767 range** by default. Pick `80` or `8080` and it's rejected as out of range.
- A NodePort is a *superset* of ClusterIP — it still gets an internal ClusterIP too. It doesn't replace the internal access, it adds external access on top.
- The doorbell opens on **every** node, not just the one running the pod; hitting any node's IP:30080 works.
- Don't confuse the three ports: outsiders use `nodePort`, in-cluster clients use `port`, and both ultimately forward to `targetPort` on the pod.
- If you build it imperatively with `create service nodeport`, double-check the selector is `app=web` — set it explicitly, since the generated one may not match.
questions.deepDive:
## NodePort on a pinned port — full rundown

### Mental model
A **NodePort** Service exposes the Service on a static port on **every node's IP**. External traffic to `<anyNodeIP>:<nodePort>` is forwarded (via kube-proxy) to the Service's ClusterIP and on to a backing pod. NodePort builds *on top of* ClusterIP — it still has an internal ClusterIP.

### The three ports
| Field | Reached by | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `nodePort` | external clients, on any node IP | 30080 |
| `port` | in-cluster clients, on the ClusterIP | 80 |
| `targetPort` | the container | 80 |

Flow: `NodeIP:30080` → `ClusterIP:80` → `podIP:targetPort`.

### Create it
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-np, namespace: svcnet-learn }
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
    nodePort: 30080        # pinned; omit to auto-assign
```
Imperative (then confirm/patch selector):
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn create service nodeport web-np --tcp=80:80 --node-port=30080
kubectl -n svcnet-learn patch svc web-np -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"web"}}}'
```

### The node-port range
| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| default range | **30000–32767** |
| configurable via | kube-apiserver `--service-node-port-range` |
| out of range | rejected: `provided port is not in the valid range` |

Omitting `nodePort` lets the control plane auto-assign one from the range.

### Service type ladder
| Type | Adds |
|---|---|
| `ClusterIP` | internal virtual IP |
| `NodePort` | ClusterIP **+** static port on every node |
| `LoadBalancer` | NodePort **+** cloud external LB |

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-np              # TYPE NodePort, PORT(S) 80:30080/TCP
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-np -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints web-np
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **nodePort must be 30000–32767** by default. Using 80/8080 fails.
- NodePort opens the port on **all** nodes, regardless of where pods run.
- It does **not** remove internal access — ClusterIP:port still works.
- The imperative `create service nodeport` may not set the selector you need — verify and patch.
- `--tcp=80:80` is `port:targetPort`; `--node-port` sets the nodePort separately.
- Don't conflate `port` (service), `targetPort` (pod), `nodePort` (node).

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80, nodePort: 30080 } ]
```
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-np -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}'
```

questions.title: Headless Service
questions.teach:
A **headless** Service sets `clusterIP: None` — no virtual IP; DNS returns the pod IPs directly. That one field is all that makes a Service headless.

**Gotcha:** it's `None` (the string), not an empty value or omitting the field.
questions.prompt:
Create a **headless** Service `web-hl` for `app=web` on `port: 80` (`clusterIP: None`).

Target: `web-hl` has `clusterIP: None` and selector app=web.
questions.hint: Set `clusterIP: None` in the Service spec.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-hl, namespace: svcnet-learn }
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80 } ]
YAML
questions.eli5:
Most Services are like a front desk with **one phone number** that secretly fans calls out to whichever employee is free — you dial the desk, you have no idea which person you reached. A **headless** Service throws away the single desk number and instead just **hands you the whole staff directory**: dial the Service name in DNS and you get back the individual phone numbers (IPs) of *every* pod directly.

You make a Service headless with exactly one setting: **`clusterIP: None`**. That's it — no virtual IP is allocated, and DNS returns the pod IPs instead of one desk number.

Why do this? When a client needs to talk to *specific* pods rather than "any one of them" — classically **StatefulSets** (databases where pod-0 and pod-1 are different), or clients that want to do their own load-balancing.

`clusterIP: None` + `selector: app=web` + a port, and you're done.

**Watch out for:**

- It must be the literal string **`None`** (capital N). Leaving the field empty, or omitting it, gives you a normal ClusterIP — not headless. `none` or `""` won't work.
- A headless Service has **no virtual IP**, so there's nothing to load-balance through and no single IP to curl. You reach pods by their individual IPs / DNS records.
- It still needs a **selector** (and matching pods) for DNS to return anything useful; a selector-less headless Service is a different, manual-endpoints case.
- Don't set `type: ...` to something exotic — headless is just a ClusterIP with the IP turned off.
questions.deepDive:
## Headless Service — full rundown

### Mental model
A **headless** Service has **no cluster virtual IP**. Instead of load-balancing through a single VIP, DNS for the Service name returns the **A/AAAA records of the backing pods directly**. You opt in with one field: `clusterIP: None`.

### Create it
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web-hl, namespace: svcnet-learn }
spec:
  clusterIP: None          # the ONLY thing that makes it headless
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
```

### Normal vs headless DNS
| | Normal ClusterIP | Headless (`clusterIP: None`) |
|---|---|---|
| Virtual IP | one allocated | **none** |
| DNS `web-hl.ns.svc` resolves to | the single ClusterIP | **all pod IPs** (multiple A records) |
| Load balancing | kube-proxy spreads across pods | client picks / round-robins DNS |
| Typical use | stateless services | StatefulSets, client-side LB, service discovery |

### With a selector (this case)
Kubernetes still creates Endpoints/EndpointSlices for the matching pods; DNS returns each pod IP. With a **StatefulSet**, each pod also gets a stable per-pod DNS name:
```
<pod>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local      e.g. web-0.web-hl.svcnet-learn.svc.cluster.local
```

### Without a selector
A headless Service **without** a selector returns whatever endpoints you define manually (EndpointSlice) — used for external/stateful backends.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-hl                 # CLUSTER-IP shows "None"
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-hl -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}{"\n"}'   # None
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get endpoints web-hl           # pod IPs listed
# DNS check from a pod:
kubectl -n svcnet-learn run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  -- nslookup web-hl.svcnet-learn.svc.cluster.local
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- Must be the literal string **`None`** (capitalised). `""`, `none`, or omitting the field → a *normal* ClusterIP, not headless.
- Headless has **no VIP** — you can't `curl` a single service IP; reach pods individually.
- `kubectl expose` doesn't set `clusterIP: None` — write YAML or `kubectl create svc clusterip web-hl --clusterip=None` (then add selector/ports).
- Still needs a selector (+ pods) for DNS to return addresses, unless you're doing manual endpoints.
- Headless is orthogonal to `type`; it's a ClusterIP Service with the IP suppressed.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector: { app: web }
  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80 } ]
```
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc web-hl -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'   # None
```

questions.title: ExternalName Service
questions.teach:
An **ExternalName** Service maps a cluster DNS name to an external one via a CNAME. Set `type: ExternalName` and `externalName: db.example.com`.

**Gotcha:** it needs no selector or ports — just the two fields.
questions.prompt:
Create an **ExternalName** Service `db-ext` that points to `db.example.com`.

Target: `db-ext` type ExternalName, externalName `db.example.com`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n svcnet-learn create service externalname db-ext --external-name db.example.com`.
questions.solution: kubectl -n svcnet-learn create service externalname db-ext --external-name db.example.com
questions.eli5:
Imagine you have a company directory, and you want everyone to be able to look up "database" and be quietly redirected to an outside partner's phone number. An **ExternalName** Service does exactly that: it's a cluster DNS entry that's really just a **redirect sign** (a CNAME) pointing from an in-cluster name to an **external** DNS name.

So `db-ext` in the cluster becomes an alias for `db.example.com`. When a pod looks up `db-ext`, DNS says "actually, go ask for `db.example.com`" and the pod connects to the real external host — without anyone hard-coding the external name in their app.

`kubectl create service externalname db-ext --external-name db.example.com -n svcnet-learn` is the whole thing.

What makes it unusual: it has **no pods, no selector, no ClusterIP, no real ports** — it never proxies traffic. It's pure DNS redirection.

**Watch out for:**

- It needs just **two fields**: `type: ExternalName` and `externalName: db.example.com`. No selector, no endpoints — adding them is pointless (and a selector is ignored).
- Because it's a **CNAME**, the target must be a **DNS name**, not an IP address. Pointing `externalName` at `10.0.0.5` won't behave like a CNAME. (For an IP, use a selector-less Service + manual endpoints instead.)
- There's **no port remapping and no load-balancing** — DNS just hands back the external name; the client connects wherever that resolves, on whatever port the client uses.
- It does no TLS or health-checking; it's a dumb alias. Whatever the external name points to is entirely on you.
questions.deepDive:
## ExternalName Service — full rundown

### Mental model
`type: ExternalName` maps an in-cluster DNS name to an **external DNS name** via a **CNAME** record. It is pure DNS indirection: **no ClusterIP, no selector, no endpoints, no proxying**. Apps use a stable internal name; you can repoint the real target without changing the app.

### Create it
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn create service externalname db-ext --external-name db.example.com
```
YAML:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: db-ext, namespace: svcnet-learn }
spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: db.example.com
```

### What resolution looks like
```
db-ext.svcnet-learn.svc.cluster.local.   CNAME   db.example.com.
```
A pod connecting to `db-ext` is redirected by DNS to `db.example.com`, then connects to whatever that resolves to.

### How it differs from every other type
| Aspect | ClusterIP/NodePort | **ExternalName** |
|---|---|---|
| Virtual IP | yes | **none** |
| Selector | yes | **none (ignored)** |
| Endpoints | yes | **none** |
| kube-proxy involvement | yes | **none** — DNS only |
| Target | in-cluster pods | **external DNS name** |

### When to use vs alternatives
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Alias to an external **hostname** | ExternalName |
| Alias to an external **IP** | selector-less Service **+** manual EndpointSlice |
| Front in-cluster pods | ClusterIP/NodePort |

> ExternalName target must be a **DNS name**. A bare IP won't form a valid CNAME.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc db-ext                 # TYPE ExternalName, EXTERNAL-IP db.example.com
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc db-ext -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalName}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n svcnet-learn run t --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \
  -- nslookup db-ext.svcnet-learn.svc.cluster.local
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- Needs only **two fields**: `type: ExternalName` + `externalName`. No ports/selector required (a selector is ignored).
- **Target is a DNS name, not an IP** — use manual endpoints for IPs.
- **No port remapping or load balancing** — it just hands back a name.
- Some older clients cache CNAMEs oddly; it's a DNS feature, not a proxy.
- `kubectl create service externalname <name> --external-name <host>` is the fastest path.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n svcnet-learn create service externalname db-ext --external-name db.example.com
kubectl -n svcnet-learn get svc db-ext -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalName}'
```
